newsitem.title: USA: Lili still a hurricane, stronger, in open Atlantic.
newsitem.headline: Lili still a hurricane, stronger, in open Atlantic.

text.p: Hurricane Lili gained strength as it neared the Azores in the Atlantic on Friday and forecasters said it could bring heavy winds and rains to Europe within three to four days.
At 11 a.m. EDT (0300 GMT), Lili's centre was near latitude 36.3 north and longitude 44.2 west, or about 860 miles (1,400 km) west-southwest of the Azores.

The hurricane's maximum sustained winds were near 100 mph (160 kph), making it a Category 2 hurricane. The storm was moving toward the east-northeast near 23 mph (37 kph), a track that would take it just north and very close to the island of Flores in the Azores.
Lili is forecast to pass close to the Azores in the next 24 to 36 hours, the National Hurricane Centre said.
Forecasters said they expected Lili would become a non-tropical winter storm as it passed over cooler waters, possibly bringing high winds and rains to Europe within several days.
With a population of about 250,000 people, Portugal's Azores are in the north Atlantic about 800 miles (1200 km) west of Portugal.
Forecasters noted that Lili had been a hurricane for seven days, which was unusual for late October. The six-month Atlantic hurricane season ends on Nov. 30.

Lili formed off the coast of Central America last week, spawning high winds and flooding that was blamed for 10 deaths in Nicaragua, Honduras and Costa Rica. It hit Cuba a week ago, causing extensive damage to agriculture and making thousands homeless, and then headed east to wreak havoc in the central Bahamas with 90 mph (145 kph) winds.
